title: Air Force Intelligence
notes: Open with the hook. You have three to four minutes in total, so do not spend any of it explaining the title.
One sentence to land early: a commander cannot act on what they do not know, and intelligence officers are the people who find out.

title: What we’ll cover
notes: This is a roadmap. Name the six topics in one sentence and move on. Reading every card aloud costs time you do not have.
If you run short on time, cut this slide first and go straight from the title to the next one.

title: Where Intel fits Air Force-wide
notes: Squadron and wing level: at a flying wing the intelligence flight normally sits in the Operations Support Squadron, under the Operations Group. Some intelligence officers are attached to a flying squadron itself. [Sources 7, 18]

MAJCOM level: a MAJCOM is a major command. Examples are Air Combat Command (ACC), Air Mobility Command (AMC), Air Force Special Operations Command (AFSOC), and Pacific Air Forces (PACAF). ACC calls itself the lead command for fighter, command and control, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance. MAJCOM intelligence staffs oversee training, qualification, and standards for their units. [Source 19]

Be careful with one old phrase: the earlier version of this slide said MAJCOMs "set intelligence requirements and priorities." That is an oversimplification. During an operation, the priorities come from the commander being supported, through that commander’s priority intelligence requirements. [Sources 1, 19]

National level: NASIC (National Air and Space Intelligence Center) is at Wright-Patterson AFB, Ohio. It characterizes foreign air, space, missile, and cyber threats and also exploits captured foreign equipment. Its heritage goes back to 1917 at McCook Field. In World War II its predecessors studied captured enemy aircraft at Wright Field. [Source 20]

DIA provides military intelligence to warfighters and defense policymakers. NSA leads U.S. signals intelligence and cybersecurity. NGA’s director is the national functional manager for geospatial intelligence. NSIC is the Space Force’s intelligence center, also at Wright-Patterson. None of these is an Air Force-only organization, except NASIC. [Source 21]

title: Requirements
notes: Degree: airforce.com asks for a bachelor’s degree in one of these fields: science, humanities, social sciences, structured analysis, engineering, or mathematics. That covers most majors, but it is not the same as "any degree." The officer directory points to a 14N education matrix that is not public, so confirm the exact list with your detachment. Also on airforce.com: a passing AFOQT score. [Sources 7, 1]

Citizenship: the 14N pages do not say it in so many words. It comes from two rules above them. Federal law limits a regular commission to U.S. citizens (10 U.S.C. 532), and intelligence community policy says anyone who needs SCI access must be a U.S. citizen (ICD 704). [Source 11]

Tier 5: this is the investigation that used to be called an SSBI. The 2016 officer directory said SSBI; the current one says Tier 5. It looks back up to 10 years for where you lived, worked, and went to school, and 7 years for things like foreign contacts and finances. It includes an Enhanced Subject Interview with you, plus record checks and interviews with references. [Sources 1, 12]

Timing: the old figure of 12–24 months reflects the backlog of 2018 and 2019, when end-to-end Top Secret cases took about 410 days. Government data for fiscal 2026 show the investigation step itself at about 60 days. The whole process for the fastest 90 percent of cases reads around five months off the chart. That last figure is read from a chart, so say "around five months." No official source gives a separate number for SCI. SCI access and a polygraph can add time. [Source 13]
You can get the entry-level AFSC before the investigation finishes, if you hold an interim Top Secret clearance. The officer directory says so directly. [Source 1]

No prior experience: the entry requirement is completing the Intelligence Officer Initial Skills Course, which you take after commissioning. Nothing in the directory asks for prior intelligence work. [Source 1]

SEIs, in plain terms: DAFMAN 36-2100 says SEIs "identify special experience and training not otherwise identified" and that they are "not substitutes for AFSCs." An officer SEI is a three-character code: one activity-code character and a two-character experience set. The officer directory says SEIs carry no AFSC restrictions, so a code is not tied to one career field. A unit commander awards an SEI once you meet its criteria. Once awarded it stays on your record and does not expire, though it can be withdrawn if you lose the qualification, for example by losing your clearance. So a 14N who earns an SEI is still a 14N. [Sources 1, 3]

An officer SEI is not even tied to a specialty. DAFMAN 36-2100 says the personnel system has no way to associate officer SEIs with AFSCs. You earn one by meeting its training and experience criteria, not just by sitting in a coded job. [Source 3]

Which SEIs 14Ns can earn: the current officer SEI tables are behind a Common Access Card login, so they cannot be checked from outside. The only published list I could open is the 2010 officer directory. Its experience sets for 14N include targeting, analysis, collection management, HUMINT, SIGINT, MASINT, imagery, geospatial, ISR operations, space, and special operations. It has nothing for "special access programs." The earlier version of this slide listed that, so it came off. [Source 22]

title: The training pipeline
notes: Course length: say "several months." The earlier version of this slide said 8.5 weeks, and that number was wrong for this course. On airforce.com, 8.5 weeks is the length of Officer Training School at Maxwell AFB, Alabama. The page never mentions the intelligence course or Goodfellow. [Source 7]

No official source I could reach gives the real length. The best estimate is about six months, from a cadet-detachment AFSC guide, and a 2020 Guard vacancy notice gives about 26 weeks. Other websites say about four months and about eight weeks. A redesign of the course, called Learning Next, began as a beta in 2018. Ask your cadre or anyone who has been through it. [Sources 8, 16, 17]

Official course names: the officer directory calls it the "Intelligence Officer Initial Skills Course." Goodfellow’s fact sheet lists it as the "14N1 – Intelligence Officer Course," taught by the 315th Training Squadron. [Sources 1, 8]

Skill levels: 14N1 is awarded when you finish that course. 14N3, the fully qualified level, needs mission qualification (the directory names IQT/MQT and mission certification) and at least 36 months performing intelligence functions. An older 2002 training plan says 18 months. The current directory says 36. [Source 1]

First assignment: at a flying wing, the intelligence flight normally sits in the Operations Support Squadron under the Operations Group. Some officers are attached to a flying squadron instead. [Sources 7, 18]

Goodfellow: the 17th Training Group says it trains all of the Air Force’s intelligence courses. Some training is delivered elsewhere, such as language training at the Defense Language Institute in Monterey and human intelligence training at Fort Huachuca. For scale, the 315th Training Squadron trains more than 3,300 students a year with over 220 permanent staff. [Source 8]

title: Why intel exists
notes: About the heading: this slide used to be titled "The Mission." That was the earlier writer’s label, not an official mission. The Air Force’s mission statement is "to fly, fight, and win…airpower anytime, anywhere" (released 8 April 2021). "My mission is to Fly, Fight, and Win" is a line from the Airman’s Creed (2007). Intelligence officers do not have a separate mission statement. What the Air Force does publish for the 14N is the specialty summary in the officer directory, and the sentence on this slide comes from it. [Sources 1, 23]

The official sentence is: "Leads and performs intelligence activities across the full range of military operations supporting the Air Force’s Service Core Function (SCF) of Global Integrated Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance (ISR)." The rest of the slide paraphrases duties 2.4 and 2.5 in the same directory. The headline, "how the Air Force knows what it doesn’t know," is a slogan we wrote, not Air Force wording. [Source 1]

OODA: Colonel John Boyd was an Air Force fighter pilot who retired in 1975. The loop appears in his briefing "Patterns of Conflict." The best-known version of that briefing is dated December 1986. His 1976 essay "Destruction and Creation" does not mention the loop. [Source 15]

Boyd and Korea: Boyd used the F-86 against the MiG-15 as an example, even though the MiG could climb higher and faster. Accounts of his reasoning credit two things about the F-86: its bubble canopy, which let pilots see more, and its fully hydraulic flight controls, which let them change maneuvers faster. So it was a faster observe-and-act cycle. It is not correct to say hardware did not matter. Avoid quoting a kill ratio. Published figures such as 8 to 1 and 10 to 1 were later revised downward. [Sources 15, 24]

Decision advantage: the Air Force’s ISR strategic vision from about 2013 is titled "AF ISR 2023: Delivering Decision Advantage." It says ISR should lead to "compressed observe, orient, decide, and act (OODA) loops." AFDP 2-0 (May 2026) defines decision advantage as "the ability to make better, faster, and more effective decisions than an adversary." I could not confirm that the current National Intelligence Strategy uses the phrase, so credit it to Air Force doctrine. [Sources 4, 6]
The line "intelligence feeds the Orient step" is our own way of connecting the two ideas. It is a fair reading, but it is not a quotation from Boyd or from doctrine.

title: The officer role, and the team beside it
notes: Officer duties come from the officer directory. It says officers "direct, plan, manage, and conduct" intelligence activities, serve as "the commander’s senior intelligence advisor," lead Airmen through the intelligence process, produce fused all-source analysis, and manage collection. Do not say officers brief aircrew "before every mission." No official source says that. Enlisted analysts also brief before missions. Say "briefs commanders and aircrew." [Source 1]

The enlisted side is a family of specialties, not just 1N0X1. From the enlisted directory: 1N0X1 All Source Intelligence Analyst; 1N1X1 Geospatial Intelligence; 1N2X1 Signals Intelligence; 1N3X1 Cryptologic Language Analyst; 1N4X1 Cyber Intelligence; 1N4X2 Cryptologic Analyst and Reporter; 1N7X1 Human Intelligence Specialist; 1N8X1 Targeting Analyst. [Source 2]

Reading the codes: in 14N, the 1 is the career group (Operations), the 14 is the utilization field (intelligence and information operations), the N is a functional-area letter, and the last digit is the skill level. DAFMAN 36-2100 does not say the N stands for a word, and I found no official source that gives it a meaning. Say "it is a classification code." Also, 14 is not "operations support." That is the 16-series. [Source 3]

Rank: new officers commission as second lieutenants. Promotion to first lieutenant and captain is close to automatic for officers in good standing, but it is not guaranteed. An officer can be found not qualified, and captain goes through a promotion process with selects and non-selects. The first truly competitive board is for major. [Source 25]

title: The five main collection disciplines (“INTs”)
notes: Who performs the INTs? The sources support a split that is close to, but not exactly, "enlisted perform and officers fuse." On the enlisted side, the specialties are mostly organized by discipline: geospatial (1N1), signals (1N2), language (1N3), cyber (1N4), and human intelligence (1N7), plus all-source (1N0) and targeting (1N8). No enlisted specialty is titled MASINT or OSINT. [Source 2]

On the officer side there is one AFSC, 14N, with no discipline shredouts. The directory says officers use "subject matter expertise in the six intelligence disciplines" and lead Airmen through the intelligence process. It also has officers doing hands-on work: producing fused all-source analysis and "directing, scheduling, and controlling specific collection platforms, sensors and HUMINT sources." RAND’s 2009 study says nine older officer specialties were merged into the single 14N in 1994 to produce "broadened specialists." Officers can still build depth in one area through assignments and SEIs. [Sources 1, 26]

Why the slide says "five main": the officer directory lists six disciplines, adding technical intelligence (TECHINT), which is the exploitation of foreign equipment. Joint doctrine (JP 2-0, 2013 edition) lists seven by adding counterintelligence. In the Air Force, counterintelligence belongs to the Special Investigations career area (OSI), not to 14N. [Sources 1, 9]

SIGINT has three sub-types, not two: communications intelligence (COMINT), electronic intelligence (ELINT, such as radar emissions), and foreign instrumentation signals intelligence (FISINT, such as missile telemetry). [Source 9]
GEOINT is imagery, imagery intelligence, and geospatial information, which includes mapping, charting, and geodetic data. NGA’s director is the national functional manager for it. [Sources 9, 21]

HUMINT: a government OPSEC handbook calls it "the oldest method for collecting information about a foreign power" and notes that most of it is collected openly by diplomats and attachés. That handbook is from 1996, so attribute the phrase to it. [Source 27]

MASINT is measurement of the physical attributes of targets and events to characterize and identify them. Careful with the "radar fingerprint" example: identifying a specific radar by its signal is also called technical ELINT. An engine or aircraft signature is a cleaner MASINT example. [Source 9]

OSINT: the 2024 intelligence community OSINT strategy says it is "increasingly important and growing in demand." Reporting credits social media and commercial satellite imagery. "Enormously" is our word, not a measured fact. [Source 28]

title: The four areas a 14N builds depth in
notes: These four are what the officer directory calls the "functional competencies" of the 14N: Analysis, Collection, Targeting, and Sensing Grid Activities. They replace the earlier slide, which listed four "specialty tracks." Two of those four were not tracks at all. [Source 1]

Where the old slide went wrong: "Fusion Analyst" is not a 14N track. The enlisted specialty 1N4X1 is titled Cyber Intelligence in the enlisted directory. A 2026 Guard vacancy notice used "Fusion Analyst" as a job title for a 1N4X1 position. The phrase "works the same layer as all-source" does not appear in Air Force or joint publications, so it has been removed. "HUMINT / Special Access" was two unrelated things on one card. [Sources 2, 29]

Targeting: the directory says officers perform "kinetic and non-kinetic target development, weaponeering, precision point mensuration, force application, execution planning, and combat assessment." Enlisted targeteers are 1N8X1 Targeting Analysts, a career field that dates to about 2019. Officers who go deep in targeting can earn a targeting SEI. [Sources 1, 2]
Collection: the directory says officers convert intelligence requirements into collection requirements, set priorities, task collection sources, monitor results, and re-task as needed. [Source 1]

Sensing Grid Activities: this is the newest item. Older material, including the 2016 directory, lists "Integration" as the fourth competency instead. If someone quotes an older list, that is why. [Source 1]

HUMINT in the Air Force is small. There is an enlisted HUMINT specialty (1N7X1, created in 2015) and officers can earn a HUMINT SEI, but most Defense Department HUMINT belongs to DIA’s Defense Clandestine Service and the Army. Army doctrine says the Air Force and Navy "have limited HUMINT collection capability." [Sources 2, 14]

Special access: a Special Access Program is a program with safeguards beyond those normally required for classified information. Access requires a formal indoctrination, and a polygraph may be required. It is a security arrangement, not an intelligence discipline or a career track. [Source 30]

title: All-source analysis: the real job
notes: The joint definition of all-source intelligence, from JP 2-0 and the DoD Dictionary, is: "Intelligence products and/or organizations and activities that incorporate all sources of information in the production of finished intelligence." The earlier notes listed the INTs inside the definition. The real definition does not, so that was not the doctrinal wording. [Sources 9, 10]

Trusting sources: analysts grade the reliability of a source and the credibility of the information separately. The scale is A through F for reliability and 1 through 6 for information. A B2 report is from a usually reliable source and is probably true. An F or a 6 means "cannot be judged," which is not the same as false. U.S. Army doctrine (FM 2-22.3) prints this scale. The names "Admiralty System" and "NATO system" come from secondary sources, because the NATO publication is not public. [Source 14]

Stating confidence: intelligence community standards (ICD 203) require fixed likelihood words, from "almost no chance" through "almost certain," each tied to a probability band. They also say not to mix a confidence level and a likelihood in the same sentence. [Source 11]

Fighting bias: Analysis of Competing Hypotheses, developed by Richards Heuer, asks the analyst to look for evidence that disconfirms each explanation instead of only supporting the first one. The U.S. Government’s 2009 Tradecraft Primer lists it with the key assumptions check and red team analysis. [Source 31]

title: A day in the life
notes: Where this comes from: the four rows are the parts of the day that have official sources. They do not describe a clock schedule. The earlier brief gave a "realistic day" by time (early morning, mid-morning, and so on). No source supports those times, so do not present them as fact.

Pre-mission briefing: a 2019 Lakenheath article describes the intelligence step-brief before a sortie and the debrief afterward. A 2019 Little Rock article calls pre-mission briefings the core objective of the 19th Operations Support Squadron intelligence section. The 1N0X1 training plan lists "Prepare and Present a Pre-Mission Briefing" as a core task. [Sources 5, 32, 33]
Analysis and production: the officer directory says officers produce "timely and accurate fused intelligence analysis" and direct intelligence activities and organizations. [Source 1]
Debrief: the 1N0X1 training plan lists "Conduct Debriefing / Prepare Mission Report (MISREP)." The debrief captures what the aircrew observed and feeds it back into collection. [Sources 5, 32]

More that is sourced: the AFROTC AFSC guide lists a 14N’s daily duties as "Read reports, network with fellow Intelligence Officers, refine data, build briefs, brief warfighters and decision-makers." A 2020 Altus AFB article describes pre-deployment threat briefs and Isolated Personnel Reports (ISOPREPs), which are also in the 1N0X1 training plan. [Sources 17, 18, 5]

Hours: the line "the day follows the flying schedule" is our summary, not a quotation. It follows from briefs and debriefs happening around flying. For deployed and real-world operations, a 2007 Air Force article says the 379th Air Expeditionary Wing intelligence flight "runs 24/7" and its squadron teams did too. I found no official source that says home-station shops work rotating 24/7 shifts, so say "deployed and real-world operations centers run 24/7." The word "overnight" came off the slide for the same reason. [Source 18]

SCIF: a SCIF is an accredited facility where sensitive compartmented information is processed, stored, and discussed. The security office decides which electronics may go in. In practice, personal phones and smartwatches stay outside. [Source 34]
Ask your cadre if someone presses you on a typical day. They can describe it from experience, and you can say the rows above come from official duty descriptions.

title: In their own words (not used)
notes: This slide is not part of the talk. It is kept at the end for reference.
Sun Tzu quotes match the Lionel Giles translation (1910): Chapter 1, "All warfare is based on deception," and Chapter 13, "Knowledge of the enemy’s dispositions can only be obtained from other men."

Churchill: the official U.S. minutes of the Tehran Conference (30 November 1943) record him saying "truth deserves a bodyguard of lies." The polished wording on the slide, "In wartime, truth is so precious that she should always be attended by a bodyguard of lies," comes from his later memoir, "Closing the Ring." [Source 35]
